title: Explaining a solution to technical and business audiences
objectives: Explain one Salesforce solution in two registers: business outcome versus technical mechanism, without inventing a second design.
Keep Well-Architected readability: a business-capability view and a technical-implementation view of the same solution.
Give VP and developer audiences the same complexity and one shared security sentence.
Name metadata versus data when explaining whether a change is a deploy, a record edit, or both.
diagnostic_question: A VP and a developer both ask you to explain the same Salesforce solution. What do you say in each register, which security sentence stays identical, and how do you keep metadata versus data from being mixed?
definition: Explaining a solution to technical and business audiences is the interview and workplace skill of rendering one Salesforce design in two registers: a business-outcome register (who is unblocked, what value, what risk) and a technical-mechanism register (objects, automation, metadata, limits). Trailhead teaches that you can vary how you tell a career story by listener while keeping the same structure, and Well-Architected Easy/Intentional asks that features be transparent to business and technology stakeholders alike, with diagrams for business capabilities and for technical implementation details. ([Land Your Next Opportunity](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/career-development-planning/land-your-next-opportunity); [Well-Architected overview](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/overview); [Intentional / readability](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/intentional))
why_it_matters: Interviewers and stakeholders fail candidates who give the VP a 'simple checkbox' and the developer a twelve-object rebuild as if both were true. Contradictory complexity, a missing shared security sentence, and mixing metadata with data create false buy-in, unsafe access stories, and surprise production impact.
sixty_second_explanation: Picture a simultaneous-interpretation booth: one speech, two headsets. The Salesforce solution is the speech. The business headset hears outcome, users, value, and risk. The technical headset hears objects, Flow or Apex, metadata versus records, and limits. You do not write a second speech. Both headsets hear the same security sentence. If the VP hears 'easy' and the developer hears 'a quarter of custom objects,' you left the booth and started two rallies.
deeper_explanation: Trailhead's Interview Strategies module prepares you to research, practice an elevator pitch, and use the CAR method (Challenge, Action, Result) so a solution walkthrough stays followable. CAR is the spine; two registers are the headsets you plug in for a mixed panel. ([Interview Strategies](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/interview-strategies))

Land Your Next Opportunity says you can have slightly different versions of your pitch depending on who you are talking to, with the same basic structure: who you are, why, skills, and an ask. Translating a Salesforce solution uses that same rule: vary register, not facts. Accomplishments should name a Salesforce result, not only 'automated processes.' ([Land Your Next Opportunity](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/career-development-planning/land-your-next-opportunity))

Salesforce Well-Architected organizes healthy solutions as Trusted, Easy, and Adaptable. Easy includes Intentional work, and Intentional includes Readability. Trusted solutions protect stakeholders—so the security sentence is not optional color for the technical headset only. ([Well-Architected overview](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/overview))

Intentional architectures prioritize and deliver features in ways that are transparent to business and technology stakeholders alike. Readability is consistency that lets people understand how things work; patterns include diagrams for business capabilities and technical implementation details, plus clear descriptions on code and declarative customizations. An anti-pattern is a what/how/why that is hard to find. ([Intentional](https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/well-architected/guide/intentional))

The Admin career path frames admins as managing users, data, and automation so systems stay secure and deliver value to the business. The Developer career path quotes builders who solve real business problems, not only compile classes. Architect Quick Look orients you on architect skills for that translation job. Explaining a solution is how those hats talk in one room. ([Admin path](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/career-path/admin); [Developer path](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/career-path/developer); [Architect Quick Look](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-architect-role-quick-look))

mental_model.analogy: A simultaneous-interpretation booth: one speech (the Salesforce solution), two headsets (business outcome versus technical mechanism), and a shared security card both listeners hear.
useful_mapping: one speech → one Salesforce solution, one complexity, one risk
business headset → outcome, users, value, time-to-value, operational risk
technical headset → objects, fields, automation, limits, metadata versus data
shared security card → one sentence both audiences hear unchanged (who can see, who cannot)
booth script → solution overview and decision record (what/how/why)
live hall performance → data (records, DML, backfill)
printed script / score → metadata (Flow, validation rule, Apex, layout)
leaving the booth for two rallies → contradictory complexity told to VP versus developer
where_it_breaks: A real interpreter may compress; you still may not drop security, volume, or whether records change.
A one-slide VP update is a shorter headset, not a license to call a multi-object design 'just a checkbox.'
Two headsets are two registers of one truth, not two approved architectures.
Interview timeboxes still need the shared security sentence; 'we ran out of time' is not an access model.
The booth does not replace org edition, license, or sharing design; those stay Needs verification when unnamed.

teach_back_prompt: Pick one Salesforce solution. Deliver it from the simultaneous-interpretation booth: ninety seconds on the business headset, ninety seconds on the technical headset, then one shared security sentence spoken twice unchanged. Name whether you described a metadata change, a data change, or both, and state one place the booth analogy breaks.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: Same Salesforce solution, two headsets: business outcome and technical mechanism. I do not tell the VP it is simple and the developer it is huge. Both hear one security sentence. I name metadata versus data so nobody thinks a Flow deploy edits every Opportunity.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I treat explaining a solution like a simultaneous-interpretation booth. The speech is one design. For a business audience I lead with who is unblocked, what value, and what operational risk. For a technical audience I lead with objects, automation, limits, and whether we change metadata or records. Well-Architected Easy wants transparency to both stakeholder types and readability via business-capability and technical diagrams. I use CAR so the story has a challenge, an action, and a result. If I catch myself softening access for the VP, I stop and restore the shared security sentence.

terminology.plain: One Salesforce solution said two ways without becoming two designs.
terminology.precise: A paired rendering: business-outcome register and technical-mechanism register that share complexity, security, and metadata-versus-data facts.
terminology.example: VP hears 'Closed Won cannot book unreviewed revenue'; developer hears 'validation on Stage plus Legal_Status__c, same freeze.'
terminology.non_example: Telling the VP it is a checkbox and telling engineering it is a new Legal_Review__c object with three integrations.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Elevator pitch: career story tuned by listener; this term is the solution itself, not your bio.
terminology.boundary: Registers change vocabulary and order, not object count, risk, or access.

terminology.plain: The headset for who is unblocked, what value, and what risk.
terminology.precise: Explanation ordered for business audiences: users, measurable outcome, operational risk, and time-to-value, with mechanism only as needed.
terminology.example: Legal review must finish before we recognize revenue on large deals; reps see a status, not a loophole.
terminology.non_example: Listing every API name and governor limit before naming who is blocked today.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: User story: a delivery slice; the register can retell a story but is not the backlog item.
terminology.boundary: Still must not hide complexity or security to sound executive-friendly.

terminology.plain: The headset for objects, automation, limits, and deploy shape.
terminology.precise: Explanation ordered for technical audiences: objects and fields, declarative versus code, metadata versus data, and platform limits.
terminology.example: Same-record validation on Opportunity.StageName when Legal_Status__c is not Approved; no trigger required for the freeze.
terminology.non_example: Only 'we automated Salesforce' with no object or tool named.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Solution design document: the durable artifact; the register is the spoken or interview form.
terminology.boundary: Mechanism talk still includes the business outcome in one sentence so the room shares a why.

terminology.plain: One access fact both audiences hear word-for-word.
terminology.precise: A single statement of who can see or change sensitive data, including partners if relevant, that is not softened for business audiences or exaggerated for technical audiences.
terminology.example: Only Legal and named managers can read review comments; Experience Cloud partners cannot.
terminology.non_example: Telling the VP 'it is locked down' while telling developers OWD is Public Read/Write.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Field-level security setting: the platform control; the sentence is how you explain that control to mixed audiences.
terminology.boundary: If actors are unknown, say unknown; do not invent profiles. Deeper sharing design is SEC topics.

terminology.plain: People can understand how the solution works without a tribal elder.
terminology.precise: Easy / Intentional / Readability: consistency plus documentation so delivery and maintenance teams understand the system; patterns include business-capability diagrams and technical-implementation diagrams.
terminology.example: A one-page capability sketch for sales ops plus an object-and-Flow diagram for the implementation team.
terminology.non_example: Apex comments only, or a slide that says 'Salesforce magic.'
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Code formatting: part of documentation, not the whole readability practice.
terminology.boundary: Readability is architecture health, not a Setup toggle named Readability.

terminology.plain: Two audiences get two different sizes of the same work.
terminology.precise: An anti-pattern where the business audience is told the solution is trivial while the technical audience is told it is a large build, or the reverse.
terminology.example: VP slide: 'one checkbox this sprint'; engineering huddle: 'new object, platform event, and three classes.'
terminology.non_example: Telling both rooms it is a same-record validation plus a status field, with a later optional Slack want.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Phased delivery: a honest thin slice plus a named later phase is not a contradiction if both audiences hear the phases.
terminology.boundary: You may shorten the VP version; you may not change the object count or risk class.

terminology.plain: Challenge, action, result—a followable interview example.
terminology.precise: Trailhead Interview Strategies framing for examples: the challenge, what you did, and the result, so a mixed audience can follow.
terminology.example: Challenge: unreviewed Closed Won. Action: two-register design and a validation freeze. Result: UAT blocked the bad path.
terminology.non_example: A ten-minute click tour of Setup with no result.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: STAR: a neighboring interview frame; this lesson uses Trailhead's CAR wording.
terminology.boundary: CAR organizes the story; two registers still supply the facts inside Action.

terminology.plain: Did we change the org's shape, the records, or both?
terminology.precise: When explaining a solution, metadata is deployable configuration or code (Flow, validation, Apex, layout); data is record instances and DML such as backfill.
terminology.example: Deploying the validation rule is metadata; setting Legal_Status__c on existing Opportunities is data.
terminology.non_example: Saying 'we will update Salesforce' when asked whether live deals change tonight.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Change set versus report: related ALM versus analytics; the split here is shape versus instances.
terminology.boundary: Exact deployment tool (change set, DevOps Center) is a later CAREER/DEVOPS topic.

mechanics.transition: Name one solution, not two speeches
mechanics.trigger: VP, developer, or mixed panel asks 'walk me through it'
mechanics.before: Urge to simplify for one listener and overbuild for the other
mechanics.after: One solution name, one complexity class, unknowns listed
mechanics.observe: Written one-liner both audiences could accept
mechanics.failure: Checkbox story for the VP and a hidden integration for engineering

mechanics.after: Outcome, users, value, operational risk stated
mechanics.observe: A sentence a VP can repeat without Setup vocabulary
mechanics.failure: Starting with governor limits when the ask was business impact

mechanics.transition: Put on the technical headset with the same facts
mechanics.after: Objects, automation type, limits, metadata versus data
mechanics.observe: Developer can name the freeze point and the deploy shape
mechanics.failure: Mechanism that implies a different object model than the business sentence

mechanics.transition: Lock the shared security sentence and complexity match
mechanics.before: 'Locked down' versus actual OWD left unsaid
mechanics.after: Identical access sentence; complexity matches; metadata versus data labeled
mechanics.observe: The security sentence can be copied between scripts without edits
mechanics.failure: Softening access for the business audience

when_to_use: When explaining a Salesforce solution to mixed technical and business audiences in a design review or interview panel.
When a business audience asks for the outcome of a solution while a technical audience in the same room needs the mechanism.
When explaining a solution so technical audiences and business audiences hear one shared security sentence, not two access stories.
When explaining whether a solution change is metadata or data so business audiences do not think a Flow deploy edits every record.
When explaining a solution's difficulty so business audiences and technical audiences are not told contradictory complexity.
when_not_to_use: Do not keep explaining a solution only in API names when the audience is a business stakeholder who asked for outcomes and risk.
Do not keep explaining a solution as simple to business audiences while privately telling technical audiences it is a multi-object rebuild.
Do not use explaining-to-audiences skill as a substitute for finishing the Salesforce solution once both audiences already share the facts.
Do not practice explaining a solution against production customer data or real legal files for a mixed-audience rehearsal.
Do not skip explaining security to business audiences because you assume only technical audiences care about sharing and FLS.
configuration_or_code_location: Interview or design-review notes: two-register scripts plus a shared security sentence (not Setup first)
Well-Architected: Overview and Easy / Intentional / Readability (business-capability and technical diagrams)
Trailhead: Interview Strategies (CAR) and Land Your Next Opportunity (pitch versions by listener)
Trailhead career paths: Administrator, Developer, and Architect Quick Look
After the explanation is honest: sandbox metadata descriptions, solution overview, and decision records—not production DML

worked_example.scenario: In a mixed mock interview, a business VP and a technical lead both ask you to practice explaining a Salesforce solution that stops reps from marking Opportunity Closed Won until legal records a decision. You have four minutes. The room already knows CAREER-001 clarifying questions were asked: threshold is large deals, partners exist, and Slack is a want. You must keep explaining the same solution to both technical and business audiences without contradictory complexity, with one shared security sentence, and with metadata versus data named.
inputs: Mixed technical and business audiences in one panel
Unknown exact OWD; partners are in scope as a who-cannot

decisions.decision: Lead the business headset with unreviewed revenue risk, then the technical headset with a same-record status plus validation, not a new object unless history was required.
decisions.because: Both audiences must hear one complexity class; a checkbox-for-VP and child-object-for-dev would be two speeches.
decisions.rejected: Telling the VP it is a simple checkbox while telling the developer you will build Legal_Review__c and a platform event

decisions.decision: Speak one shared security sentence unchanged: only Legal and named managers see review comments; Experience Cloud partners cannot.
decisions.because: Trusted solutions protect stakeholders; softening 'locked down' for the VP hides partner risk.
decisions.rejected: Omitting partners from the VP version because it 'sounds complicated'

decisions.decision: Name metadata versus data: deploying the validation and field is metadata; stamping existing Opportunities is a data backfill with a report of leftovers.
decisions.because: Business audiences will otherwise assume tonight's live deals all change when you deploy.
decisions.rejected: Saying 'we will update Salesforce' as if deploy and backfill were the same

configuration_or_code: Do not open production Setup. Write two 90-second scripts and one security sentence.
Business register: stop booking unreviewed revenue on large deals; reps see a legal status; Slack is later.
Technical register: Opportunity field Legal_Status__c plus a validation on StageName; FLS for Legal; no trigger for the freeze.
Label deploy as metadata and any historical stamp as data; mark OWD numbers Needs verification.
worked_example.output: Two scripts, one shared security sentence, a complexity match, and a metadata-versus-data split—not a production deploy.
verification: A teammate can read both scripts and not find a different object count or risk class.
The security sentence is character-identical in both scripts, including partners.
Each script has at least one line tagged metadata and one tagged data or explicitly 'no data change tonight.'
worked_example.self_explanation: Credit comes from explaining one solution in two registers, keeping complexity and security aligned, and separating metadata from data—not from sounding more technical than the VP.

hands_on_lab.environment: A notes file plus optional Trailhead Playground with synthetic LAB_ records only. No production org and no real customer legal files.
starting_state_checks: You can name one Salesforce solution you already understand (for example a validation freeze on Closed Won)
You will not deploy metadata or run DML in a customer production org
steps: Write a one-line solution name at the top of the notes file, for example: freeze Closed Won on large LAB_ Opportunities until legal records a decision.
Draft a 90-second business-register script: audience, outcome, value, operational risk, and what will not ship (Slack as a want). Ban unexplained API names.
Draft a 90-second technical-register script for the same solution: objects, fields, automation type, limits or Needs verification, and whether Apex is required.
Write one shared security sentence that both scripts will contain verbatim, including who must not see comments if partners exist.
Diff the two scripts for contradictory complexity (object count, timeline, risk class). Rewrite until they match; shortening is allowed, a second architecture is not.
Tag one line in each script as metadata (deployable shape) and one as data (records, backfill) or write 'no data change on deploy.'

Optional playground: open a LAB_ validation rule or Flow in a sandbox and rewrite only a Description draft on paper in both registers; do not save production-like descriptions that name real customers.
guided_completion: Read the shared security sentence twice out loud and confirm the words did not change.
Point to the booth: which paragraph was the business headset and which was the technical headset.
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: Swap the solution to 'a scheduled Flow that emails legal.' Produce two registers plus a shared security sentence, and show you still refuse to tell the VP it is a simple email if the Flow also updates Opportunity fields (data) after a metadata deploy.
evidence: Notes file with two scripts, one identical security sentence, and metadata versus data tags.
A short diff note listing any complexity mismatch you found and how you fixed it.
stop_recovery_cleanup: Discard any production screenshots. Delete LAB_ description edits if you saved them in a shared sandbox by mistake.
hands_on_lab.limitations: Playground labels vary by release. Do not quote unofficial interview dumps. OWD and license facts stay Needs verification unless supplied.

decision_table.signal: Mixed room: VP asks time-to-value while the developer asks object count in the same minute
decision_table.choose: Same solution, two registers: outcome first, then mechanism
decision_table.not: Give the VP a simple-checkbox story and the developer a different architecture
decision_table.why: Well-Architected Easy expects transparency to business and technology stakeholders alike

decision_table.signal: Someone asks whether existing Opportunities will look different after tonight's release
decision_table.choose: Separate metadata deploy from data backfill in both registers
decision_table.not: Say we will update Salesforce without naming records versus Flow
decision_table.why: Business audiences hear live-deal risk; technical audiences hear DML versus metadata deploy

decision_table.signal: Security is described only as locked down with no named actors or partner path
decision_table.choose: One shared security sentence both audiences hear unchanged
decision_table.not: Soften access for the VP and reveal Public Read/Write only to developers
decision_table.why: Trusted solutions protect stakeholders; contradictory access stories are a security failure

decision_table.signal: Interviewer asks you to walk through a Salesforce solution you shipped
decision_table.choose: CAR method then two-register depth on the same facts
decision_table.not: Recite Setup clicks with no business result or skip the mechanism entirely
decision_table.why: Trailhead Interview Strategies teaches CAR so examples stay concise and followable

decision_table.signal: New hires cannot explain the solution and the what/how/why lives in one person's head
decision_table.choose: Pair a business-capability diagram with a technical implementation diagram
decision_table.not: Leave readability only in Apex comments or a single tribal expert
decision_table.why: Well-Architected readability patterns ask for both diagram types for solutions

limitations: Two-register skill is not a Salesforce Setup feature and has no edition toggle.
Well-Architected is guidance; it does not auto-grade your interview answer.
A clear explanation cannot discover license or sharing limits you still must look up in Help.
Architect Quick Look is orientation, not a complete communication curriculum.
security_notes: The shared security sentence is required even when the business audience did not ask about sharing.
Do not use real customer legal comments or production record screenshots in a rehearsal.
Partner and Experience Cloud users are a different audience than internal reps; say so in both registers.
CSS or a hidden Lightning component is not an access model to explain as 'locked down.'
common_mistakes: Telling the VP the solution is a checkbox and telling the developer it is a new object model.
Using only API names with a business audience, or only slogans with a technical audience.
Dropping the security sentence because the clock ran out.
Saying 'we will update Salesforce' when the question was metadata versus data.
Treating Slack notifications as the same complexity class as the legal freeze.
Skipping CAR so the interview example has clicks but no result.

troubleshooting.symptom: Interviewer says you dumbed it down for the VP and then described a different system to engineering
check: Is object count the same in both registers?
Did a later phase get sold as this sprint to only one audience?
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: Executives wanted a false simple story

troubleshooting.symptom: Business stakeholder still thinks tonight's deploy will rewrite every Opportunity
check: Did you tag metadata versus data out loud?
Did you say 'no backfill' or name the backfill report?
Did you separate Flow deploy from record DML?
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: They already know change sets do not stamp records

troubleshooting.symptom: Technical audience says they still do not know how it works
check: Did the mechanism register name objects and automation type?
Is there a technical-implementation sketch, not only a capability slogan?
Did you hide limits behind 'it is standard Salesforce'?
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: Developers only wanted the elevator pitch

production_notes: Put the two-register explanation and decision record where the team can search them; unread chat history is a readability anti-pattern.
Update declarative Description fields so they match what the customization actually does, in language a maintainer can read.
Sandbox first. Do not rehearse mixed-audience demos on production records.
If legal or partner data is in the story, security review belongs in both registers before any production field.

distractor_explanations.B: Business listeners should not require API names.
distractor_explanations.C: A checkbox is a stated tool, not a pitch rule.
distractor_explanations.D: Changing complexity by listener is contradictory complexity.

mcqs.prompt: Salesforce Well-Architected organizes healthy solutions around which three top-level capabilities?

options.C: Admin, Developer, and End user only
options.D: Change sets, Packages, and Scratch orgs

mcqs.rationale: The Well-Architected overview is built around Trusted, Easy, and Adaptable.

distractor_explanations.C: Career hats, not the framework's top level.

mcqs.prompt: Which pair best matches Well-Architected readability for explaining one solution?

options.A: A diagram of business capabilities and a diagram of technical implementation details
options.B: Apex comments only and no business view
options.C: A VP slide that says simple and an unpublished twelve-object design
options.D: A page layout screenshot used as the security model

mcqs.rationale: Readability patterns include diagrams for business capabilities and for technical implementation details.

distractor_explanations.B: Code-only notes are not enough for mixed stakeholders.

mcqs.prompt: A VP hears 'it is locked down' and a developer later says OWD is Public Read/Write. What failed?

options.A: The shared security sentence was not identical across audiences
options.B: The elevator pitch was longer than thirty seconds
options.C: CAR was used instead of STAR
options.D: The Admin career path was quoted

mcqs.rationale: Both audiences must hear the same access fact; Trusted solutions protect stakeholders.

distractor_explanations.B: Pitch length is not the access model.
distractor_explanations.C: This lesson uses Trailhead CAR; the failure is security mismatch.
distractor_explanations.D: Career-path framing does not cause OWD contradictions.

mcqs.prompt: You deploy a validation rule. A business stakeholder asks if existing deals change tonight. Best explanation?

options.A: The deploy is metadata; existing Opportunities change only if we run a data backfill
options.B: Validation rules always rewrite every Opportunity at deploy
options.C: Metadata and data are the same in Salesforce
options.D: Tell only the developer; the business audience does not need this split

mcqs.rationale: Explaining a solution requires naming metadata versus data so live records are not confused with a shape change.

distractor_explanations.B: Deploying a rule does not DML every record by itself.
distractor_explanations.C: Shape versus instances is the point of the split.
distractor_explanations.D: Business audiences own operational risk on live deals.

mcqs.prompt: You told the VP the freeze is a checkbox this sprint and told engineering it needs a new object, platform event, and three classes. What should you do?

options.A: Rewrite both registers so complexity matches; shortening is allowed, a second architecture is not
options.B: Keep both stories because executives need comfort
options.C: Delete the technical register so nobody can compare
options.D: Call the contradiction a two-register explanation

mcqs.rationale: Two registers are two headsets on one speech, not two designs.

distractor_explanations.C: Hiding the mechanism fails technical audiences and readability.
distractor_explanations.D: Two-register does not mean two truths.

mcqs.prompt: How should Admin and Developer career-path framings show up when you explain one solution?

options.A: Admins stress secure value to the business; developers still name how the solution solves a business problem, not only code
options.B: Admins may only speak outcomes; developers may only speak Apex
options.D: Developers should contradict admin complexity to sound senior

mcqs.rationale: Admin path: secure, efficient value. Developer path: solutions that drive real business value.

distractor_explanations.B: Each hat still uses two registers in a mixed room.
distractor_explanations.C: Admins are framed as keeping systems secure.

mcqs.prompt: What is Salesforce Architect: Quick Look primarily for in this lesson?

options.A: Orienting on what architects do and the skills they need, including translating across stakeholder types
options.B: Publishing governor-limit tables for every edition

mcqs.rationale: The module is a short role orientation on architect skills.

mcqs.prompt: Land Your Next Opportunity contrasts resume lines. Which line better supports explaining a Salesforce solution's result?

options.A: Designed an automated lead qualification process using Salesforce that resulted in a named outcome
options.C: Responsible for end-user training with no count or result

mcqs.rationale: The unit's DO column highlights accomplishments with Salesforce and a result, not vague automation claims.

distractor_explanations.B: That is the NOT example for highlighting accomplishments.
distractor_explanations.C: The unit prefers action verbs and specifics such as trained 500 users.

mcqs.prompt: A mixed panel asks you to start. Best first move for explaining the legal-freeze solution?

options.A: One-sentence outcome, then mechanism, then the shared security sentence, using CAR if they asked for an example
options.B: Open Object Manager and add a field while talking
options.C: Give the VP a checkbox and privately Slack the developer a different design
options.D: Refuse to speak until only technical people remain

mcqs.rationale: Mixed audiences get outcome then mechanism on one speech, with security locked.

distractor_explanations.B: Configuration is not the explanation skill.

mcqs.prompt: Which documentation situation is a Well-Architected readability anti-pattern when explaining solutions?

options.A: The what/how/why is hard to find and may be unavailable to most teams
options.B: People can search for and find relevant documentation
options.C: Diagrams exist for business capabilities and technical implementation details
options.D: Code and declarative customizations have clear descriptions that match behavior

mcqs.rationale: Intentional readability lists hard-to-find what/how/why as an anti-pattern.

mcqs.prompt: You have ninety seconds with only a business audience. What still must appear?

options.A: Outcome, risk, the shared security sentence, and honest complexity even if mechanism is one clause
options.C: A second, smaller architecture than you will tell developers later
options.D: No security, because they are not technical

mcqs.rationale: A shorter headset is not a second speech and not a license to drop security.

distractor_explanations.B: Limits belong mainly on the technical headset unless they change the business risk.
distractor_explanations.D: Trusted solutions protect stakeholders, including business audiences.

mcqs.prompt: A developer asks only for objects and a VP in the same call asks only for ROI. How do you avoid two truths?

options.A: Answer both from one solution: ROI from the freeze outcome, objects from the same freeze, complexity matched
options.B: Mute one stakeholder so you can specialize
options.C: Invent a higher ROI for the VP than the technical design can support
options.D: Say ROI is metadata and objects are data

mcqs.rationale: Two questions, one speech. ROI and objects must describe the same freeze.

distractor_explanations.B: Mixed audiences stay in the booth.
distractor_explanations.C: False ROI is a fact change, not a register change.
distractor_explanations.D: That misuses the metadata versus data split.

flashcards.front: What is a two-register explanation of a Salesforce solution?
flashcards.back: One design spoken as business outcome and as technical mechanism, sharing complexity, security, and metadata-versus-data facts.

flashcards.front: What is the simultaneous-interpretation booth in this lesson?
flashcards.back: One speech (the solution), two headsets (business versus technical), and a shared security card both listeners hear.

flashcards.front: What must not change when you shorten the VP version of a solution?
flashcards.back: Object count, risk class, and the shared security sentence. Shortening is not a second architecture.

flashcards.front: What is a shared security sentence?
flashcards.back: One access fact both audiences hear unchanged, including who must not see data such as partners.

flashcards.front: Name the three Well-Architected top-level capabilities.
flashcards.back: Trusted, Easy, and Adaptable. Easy includes Intentional work, and Intentional includes Readability.

flashcards.front: What two diagram types support Well-Architected readability?
flashcards.back: Diagrams for business capabilities and diagrams for technical implementation details of the same solution.

flashcards.front: What does CAR stand for on Trailhead Interview Strategies?
flashcards.back: Challenge, Action, Result—used so a solution example stays concise and followable.

flashcards.front: How does Land Your Next Opportunity treat pitch versions by listener?
flashcards.back: Slightly different versions are allowed; the basic structure stays the same. Facts do not fork.

flashcards.front: Deploying a validation rule versus stamping existing Opportunities—which is metadata and which is data?
flashcards.back: The rule deploy is metadata. Stamping records is data (DML/backfill). Do not say 'update Salesforce' for both.

flashcards.front: How does the Admin career path frame value when you explain a solution?
flashcards.back: Admins manage users, data, and automation, keep systems secure, and deliver value to the business.

flashcards.front: How should a developer explain a solution using the Developer career path framing?
flashcards.back: As a solution that drives real business value and helps teams solve a business problem, plus the mechanism.
Telling business audiences the work is trivial while telling technical audiences it is a large build, or the reverse.
The what/how/why of solutions is hard to find or unavailable to most teams.
Name one solution, business outcome, technical mechanism, shared security sentence, metadata versus data.

flashcards.front: Where does the booth analogy break?
flashcards.back: You may not drop security or live-data risk to compress, and two headsets are not two approved designs.

flashcards.front: Give a stronger accomplishment line than 'Automated processes using Salesforce.'
flashcards.back: Name the process, the Salesforce mechanism, and a result, as in the Land Your Next Opportunity DO column.

interview_questions.question: How do you explain the same Salesforce solution to a VP and to a developer?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Same solution, two registers. The VP hears outcome, users, value, and risk. The developer hears objects, automation, and limits. Complexity and security stay identical. I name metadata versus data so a deploy is not mistaken for a record rewrite.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I use a simultaneous-interpretation booth: one speech, two headsets. I will not tell the VP it is a checkbox and the developer it is a twelve-object rebuild. Well-Architected Easy wants transparency to business and technology stakeholders, and readability wants a business-capability view plus a technical-implementation view. I start with who is unblocked, then the freeze point on Opportunity, then one security sentence both people hear, including partners if they exist. If a later Slack notification is a want, both audiences hear that it is later.
interview_questions.example: VP: stop booking unreviewed revenue. Developer: Legal_Status__c plus validation on StageName. Both: partners cannot see comments.
tradeoffs: Plain language versus sounding imprecise to engineers
follow_ups: What if they are in the same meeting?
What if the VP insists it is simple?

interview_questions.question: What is a two-register explanation, and how is it not two truths?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Two registers change order and vocabulary, not object count, risk, or access. If those fork, I left the booth and started two speeches. Land Your Next Opportunity allows pitch versions by listener with the same structure; solutions follow that rule.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: The business register leads with outcome. The technical register leads with mechanism. Both must describe the same freeze, the same phase, and the same who-cannot. A phased delivery is honest if both audiences hear the phases. A checkbox-this-sprint story plus a hidden platform-event design is a fail. I will invite either listener to correct the one-sentence solution name before I go deeper.
interview_questions.example: Both rooms hear 'same-record validation this slice; child object only if history is required later.'
tradeoffs: One slice versus a roadmap dump
follow_ups: How do you document the one speech?
When is a second object model allowed?
weak_answer_warnings: Inventing a second architecture for one listener

interview_questions.question: Give a shared security sentence for a legal-review freeze that includes partners.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Only Legal and named managers can read legal review comments. Experience Cloud partners who close deals cannot see those comments. I will say that sentence to the VP and to the developer without softening it.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Trusted solutions protect stakeholders, so I do not hide partner risk from the business headset. If OWD or FLS numbers are unknown, I mark them Needs verification instead of saying locked down. The technical register can then name FLS and sharing options, but the who-can and who-cannot stay the same words. CSS hiding is not the sentence. If partners were never elicited, I say that gap rather than inventing an internal-only world.
interview_questions.example: Copied verbatim into both scripts: partners cannot read Legal_Comments__c; FLS details TBD in sandbox.
tradeoffs: Naming unknown sharing versus guessing OWD
Length of the sentence versus completeness
follow_ups: What if there are no partners?
Where does this sit versus SEC topics?

interview_questions.question: A VP asks whether existing Opportunities change when you 'push the solution.' How do you answer?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I split metadata from data. Deploying the validation rule and field is metadata. Existing deals change only if we run a backfill or users edit records. If there is no backfill, tonight's live deals keep their current field values until someone edits them.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Business audiences hear operational risk on live revenue. Technical audiences hear change set or DevOps deploy versus DML. I say which reports will show leftovers if we do backfill. I will not say we updated Salesforce as if those were one action. Admins manage users, data, and automation; mixing those three in one verb is how surprise production stories start. If they want history on old deals, that is a data project with its own security sentence.
interview_questions.example: Metadata: validation deploy. Data: optional stamp of Legal_Status__c on open Opportunities over threshold, with a leftover report.
tradeoffs: No-backfill simplicity versus incomplete historical status
Batch DML volume versus leaving old deals unlabeled
follow_ups: How do you test without production data?
weak_answer_warnings: Validation rules rewrite every record at deploy
Only the developer needs this split

interview_questions.question: How does Well-Architected readability change how you explain a solution at work, not only in interviews?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I pair a business-capability view with a technical-implementation view, keep descriptions matched to behavior, and make the what/how/why searchable. That is readability, not a slide that says Salesforce magic.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Intentional architectures are transparent to business and technology stakeholders. If only one tribal expert can explain the freeze, we have the anti-pattern. I budget time for documentation even on small declarative changes. Decision records capture options and why. In an interview I can still speak the two views without a wiki, but I will say the durable artifacts should exist. Architect Quick Look is orientation; the pattern pages are where I point for health.
interview_questions.example: A sales-ops capability sketch plus an Opportunity-and-validation diagram stored where new hires can search.
follow_ups: How do naming conventions help mixed audiences?
weak_answer_warnings: Apex comments as the only artifact

interview_questions.question: Walk through a solution you built using CAR, then show both registers.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Challenge: reps booked Closed Won while legal was still in email. Action: elicited the freeze, then a status field and validation, with FLS for Legal. Result: UAT blocked the bad path and the leftover report was empty. Business register is the revenue risk; technical register is the validation.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Interview Strategies wants CAR so the interviewer can follow. Challenge is the pain, not the checkbox. Action includes clarifying questions from CAREER-001 and then the mechanism. Result is observable, like a LAB_ Opportunity that cannot close. I then spend thirty seconds on the business headset and thirty on the technical headset without changing complexity. I include the shared security sentence in Action, not as an afterthought. If I lack a numeric result, I say so instead of inventing ROI.
interview_questions.example: CAR on a university recruiting app from Trailhead's Linda example pattern: requirements, iteration, stakeholder buy-in—then two registers for the actual Salesforce freeze you shipped.
tradeoffs: Seven or eight prepared stories versus over-rehearsed stiffness
Numeric KPI versus honest qualitative result
follow_ups: What was the challenge in one sentence?

interview_questions.question: Halfway through, you realize you told the VP it was simple and you just told the developer about three new objects. Recover.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I name the miss out loud: those were two speeches. I restore one complexity class both people can hear, split must-have freeze from later objects, and repeat the shared security sentence unchanged.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Interviewers score recovery. I do not pretend the VP slide was a different product. I say the honest slice is same-record validation now; a child object is a later phase if history is required, and both audiences hear that phase. I check metadata versus data so nobody thinks the three objects already shipped. I apologize for the fork, not for using plain language. Then I invite a correction to the one-sentence solution name.
interview_questions.example: Stop: I oversimplified. This sprint is validation plus status. The three-object model is a backlog item, not tonight's deploy.
tradeoffs: Calling a phase later versus sneaking scope back
Owning the miss versus doubling down
follow_ups: What if the VP is angry about the larger size?
What if engineering already started the three objects?
weak_answer_warnings: Hoping the VP was not listening
Blaming the developer for being too detailed

interview_questions.question: Teach explaining a Salesforce solution to mixed audiences without jargon, then name a limitation.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Imagine a simultaneous-interpretation booth: one speech, two headsets. Business headset is outcome and risk. Technical headset is how Salesforce enforces it. Both hear who cannot see the data. Metadata is the printed script; data is the live performance in the hall.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I stay with the booth: one speech, two headsets. The booth breaks if I compress away security or if I treat two headsets as two truths. Well-Architected still wants diagrams and searchable what/how/why after the meeting. Admin and developer hats both owe the business a real problem solved. Architect orientation is the translation job, not a license to keep two private designs. I end by asking the VP to repeat the outcome and the developer to name the freeze point; if they disagree, the speech is still two rallies.
interview_questions.example: Teach-back on the legal freeze with both headsets and the partner who-cannot, then 'the booth does not replace looking up licenses.'
tradeoffs: Teach-back time versus remaining interview questions
follow_ups: How do you store the speech after the meeting?
weak_answer_warnings: Two speeches instead of two headsets
